lines.text: In South Florida, in the dark, a five-foot man is moving a stone heavier than a truck. Nobody is watching. That's the legend. Eleven hundred tons of rock, raised by one man, alone, at night, for twenty-eight years.
Some say he levitated the stones, or sang to them, or bent the earth's magnetism. Some say he had help from somewhere else. His only hint? I have discovered the secrets of the pyramids.
The story always ends the same way. No witnesses. So tonight, we fix that. We stake out the yard, hour by hour, from dusk until dawn.
The subject, the yard, the claims. Then the quarry, the lift, the move and the famous gate. And at sunrise, we check who else was watching.
Every claim gets a score. At the end, a verdict. Mystery, or method. Let's begin.
Log entry one. Seven p m. The subject. Edward Leedskalnin, born in eighteen eighty-seven in Latvia. About five feet tall and a hundred pounds, in most tellings.

The legend says that at twenty-six he was engaged to a girl of sixteen, Agnes Skuvst, who called it off the day before the wedding. A Latvian researcher later reported that the girl was real, but her name was Hermine Lusis.
Ship records show him sailing from Hamburg in March nineteen twelve, in steerage, and landing in New York in April. Then a decade of heavy work: Canada, Idaho, the Oregon logging boom, a lumber mill.
Remember those jobs. He came from a family of stonemasons, and spent years in timber country, where one log can outweigh his biggest stone. That's not a frail man. That's a man who knows rigging.
Believing he had tuberculosis, he moved to South Florida. A local couple, Ruben Moser and his wife, took him in. In February nineteen twenty-three, they sold him an acre of land for ten dollars.
And under that acre lay the perfect raw material. Not coral, despite the name. Oolite. A soft, porous limestone of tiny round grains and shell, just inches under the topsoil.
So our subject is a trained mason and a seasoned logger, standing on a free quarry. Now, let's see what he built with it.
Entry two. Eight thirty. The yard. Today it's called Coral Castle, in Homestead, south of Miami. Ed called it Rock Gate. Around eleven hundred tons of stone.

An eight-foot wall of upright blocks. A two-storey tower where he lived, above his workshop. A crescent moon. Planets. A sundial. A heart-shaped table, a table shaped like Florida, rocking chairs, a bathtub, a throne. All stone.
The signs boast blocks of fifteen tons on average. Two monoliths twenty-five feet tall. A thirty-ton block crowning the north wall. And no mortar. The stones are held by their own weight.
Hold on to those figures, though. Sources don't always agree, and one investigator who visited warned that some weights on the signs are probably exaggerated.
Then there's the star of the show. A gate cut from one slab of stone, said to weigh nine tons, that swung open with the push of a single finger. By nineteen eighty, it was a TV sensation.
And Ed was not hiding any of it. He charged ten cents a visit, later twenty-five, and let you in free if you were broke. Ring the bell twice, and he came down from the tower to give the tour himself.
A public attraction, built by a man who gave the tours himself. Keep that in mind when you hear the words no witnesses. Next, the claims.

Entry three. Ten p m. The claims. Asked how he did it, Ed answered in riddles. It's not difficult, if you know how. I understand the laws of weight and leverage. And, I have discovered the secrets of the pyramids.
Believers ran with that last line. If one small man could raise thirty tons alone, maybe he had found the lost method of the ancient builders. A way to make stone weightless.
The legends grew. Teenagers supposedly spied on him and saw blocks rise like hydrogen balloons. Others claimed he laid his hands on the stones and sang, like a monk, until they lifted.

The most popular theory is magnetism. Ed really did write pamphlets about magnetic current, and he described something he called a perpetual motion holder. To some, that's the key. He cancelled gravity with magnets.
But they're not engineering manuals. They're home-made physics. His perpetual motion holder, one skeptic noted, keeps working only as long as it's plugged into electricity.
The energy theories followed. Ley lines under the yard. A grid of harmonic resonance. Richard Hoagland, of Face on Mars fame, dowsed the site and talked of energy from other dimensions.
And of course, aliens. Ancient Aliens featured Coral Castle among its mysterious structures. Books have tied it to Atlantis, the Bermuda Triangle and U F Os. If he had help, it wasn't human.
That's a lot of power for one quiet man in a flat cap. So let's stop listening to stories, and watch the work. Eleven thirty. The quarry.
Entry four. Eleven thirty. The quarry. Ed never needed to haul stone in. At Rock Gate, he cut it a few feet from his own walls. The pool and the pit by the north wall are his old quarries.
Oolite is soft enough to cut with hand tools, and it's riddled with holes. Geologists measure the Miami limestone at around forty percent empty space.
He split the blocks from the bedrock with wedges. The museum says some were old truck springs, sharpened. He cut channels with saws and chisels, then pried each block free of its bed.
His tools survive in the tower workshop. Chains, hooks, hoists, pulleys, winches, and a wheelbarrow made from a truck's brake drum. Much of it from scrap car parts.

Now, the weights. Porous stone is much lighter than granite. The gate's listed size is eighty-one by ninety-two by twenty-one inches. With the measured porosity, our math puts it at roughly four to six tons, not nine. A biologist writing in Skeptic magazine calculated about five and a half.
And yes, he worked at night. But the reason may be simpler than secrecy. This is South Florida. Cutting rock under the midday sun is brutal. A lantern after dark is just common sense.
So far, nothing strange. Soft stone, steel wedges, and a man who knows how to use them. But cutting is the easy part. Lifting it is the real question. One a m.
Entry five. One a m. The lift. And here, our stakeout gets lucky. This moment was photographed. Ed liked to pose with his work for a box Brownie camera.
The pictures show a tall tripod of three poles, like telephone poles, joined at the top, with chains and pulleys hanging from it. And under it, stone blocks, hanging in the air.

Even the museum's own history now says it plainly. He used tripod-mounted chain falls and basic block and tackle. A chain fall is a geared hoist. Pull a light chain a long way, and the heavy hook rises a short way.

That trade is the whole secret. With enough gearing, one man's pull can raise several tons. It's slow, metres of chain for every few centimetres of lift. But slow was never Ed's problem. He had twenty-eight years.
One old objection said that so many pulleys would create too much friction to move anything. Skeptic Brian Dunning compared that to saying a car can't move in first gear. Gearing down is the point.
Others say the tripods look too short for the twenty-five-foot monoliths. But you don't lift a tall stone straight up. You raise one end, pack it, and walk it upright, step by step.

In Michigan, a retired builder named Wally Wallington showed one man, with only wood, levers and gravity, raising a concrete block of over nineteen thousand pounds and standing it on end. No pulleys at all.
So the lift has photographs, tools and modern demonstrations. What it lacks is a single floating stone. Two thirty. Time to move house.

Entry six. Two thirty. The move. By the mid thirties, development was creeping toward Ed's Place in Florida City. In nineteen thirty-four, a gang of young men broke in and attacked him. He decided to leave, and take his castle with him.
In nineteen thirty-six, he bought ten acres about ten miles north, near Homestead. Then he began moving his multi-ton sculptures, one load at a time.
And here the legend says it again. People saw the stones travelling up the old Dixie Highway, but no one ever saw him load or unload them. In some versions, he moved the whole castle overnight.

Ed didn't drive. So he made a deal with a neighbouring farmer, Bob Biggers, who had a tractor and a heavy trailer. Ed loaded the stones. Biggers towed them. Then, in his sister's sworn account, Ed sent him off. Go on now, I don't want anyone to bother me while I work.
So the move had a witness, who hauled the cargo. And he left us a clue about timing. By Biggers' account, it took Ed three days just to set the obelisk upright at the new site.
The whole move took about three years. That's not the speed of levitation. That's the speed of a careful man with chains, a borrowed trailer, and enormous patience.
One mystery is left, the one people still travel to touch. Four a m. The gate.

Entry seven. Four a m. The nine-ton gate. A slab about seven feet wide, eight feet tall and twenty-one inches thick, fitting its gap in the wall within a quarter of an inch. For decades, a child could turn it with one hand.
How? Some said it sat on a natural energy point. Others, that Ed had found a perfect balance no engineer could copy. For decades, nobody could see inside.
Then, in nineteen eighty-six, it stopped turning. It took six men and a fifty-ton crane to lift it out. And inside, they found Ed's secret.

He had drilled a hole straight down through the centre of the slab, slid in a metal shaft, and set the whole thing on an old truck bearing. The bearing had rusted. That was all. One skeptic even reported it as the axle of a Model T Ford.

With a new shaft and bearing, the gate went back on July the twenty-third, nineteen eighty-six. It failed again in two thousand five and was repaired, but never turned as easily. Ed had done it alone. The modern crew needed a crane.
So the greatest mystery of Coral Castle was a well-centred hole and a salvaged bearing. Brilliant, yes. Supernatural, no. Dawn is coming. Time to ask the last question.
Entry eight. Five thirty. The witnesses. Our stakeout began with the claim that nobody ever saw him work. So, who did?

His friend Orval Irwin, a building contractor, said he watched Ed quarry stone and raise parts of his wall, and he drew the methods in a book called Mister Can't Is Dead. He called the mystical theories an insult to his friend's hard work.

Then there are the tripod photographs, and reports of a nineteen forty-four film of him at work. And visitors. By nineteen thirty-six, Ed counted more than fifteen thousand. He wasn't building in secret. He was running a business.

In late nineteen fifty-one he fell ill. He hung a sign on the gate, going to the hospital, and took the bus to Miami. He died there, aged sixty-four. In his home they found three thousand five hundred dollars, saved from dime tours.

And the aliens? In twenty-eight years of a public, photographed, ticketed project, there is no trace of them. No strange material. No unexplained tool. Only a five-foot mason, his chains, and his stone.
Sunrise. The stakeout is over. Time to file the report.

One man, building for decades: evidence. Local porous oolite, not coral: evidence. Tripods, chain falls and block and tackle, photographed: evidence. Exactly how he rigged the very biggest blocks: still open.
Nobody ever saw him work: false. Levitation, magnetism or singing stones: no evidence. Aliens, or a lost pyramid secret: no evidence.

The verdict. Method, not mystery. Coral Castle was built by one stubborn, skilled man with simple machines and almost thirty years of nights. As one investigator put it, a marvel, not a mystery. That makes it more impressive, not less.
Next case. A clay disc from Crete, stamped on both sides with symbols nobody can read. A message, a prayer, or a hoax? The Phaistos Disc.
Would you have believed the floating stones? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next case on the stakeout list.
